Prefer `sorted()` when the list came from a caller or a cache, so you do not reorder data someone else is still using.

## Verify it

Add a test that calls the function with two tasks out of order and asserts the returned titles are in due-date order, and that the input list is unchanged if you used `sorted()`.

cards.front: A flex row holds an avatar and an `.info` div. The email in `.info` has `overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap`, yet a long email still makes the row wider than the phone. Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Let the flex item shrink below its content width:

```css
.info {
  flex: 1;
  min-width: 0; /* allow shrinking; the ellipsis can now appear */
}
```

The ellipsis rules on the email then take effect.

## Why it works

Flex items start with `min-width: auto`, which for a flex item means "no narrower than my content" (its min-content size). A no-wrap email makes that minimum very wide, so `.info` refuses to shrink and the row overflows; the text never gets cut, so no ellipsis appears. `min-width: 0` (or `overflow: hidden` on `.info`, which also sets the automatic minimum to 0) lets it shrink to the space left.

## Verify it

In DevTools device mode at 320px wide, check that the row fits and the email ends with "…". In the Computed pane for `.info`, `min-width` should show `0px` instead of `auto`.

cards.front: Each task card has `transform: translateY(0)` for a hover lift. A card's dropdown menu has `position: absolute; z-index: 1000`, yet the next card is drawn on top of the menu. Why, and what is a fix?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The `transform` makes each card its own stacking context, so the menu's `z-index: 1000` only counts inside its own card. Raise the card that has the open menu:

```css
.card { position: relative; }
.card.menu-open { z-index: 1; } /* whole card, menu included, goes on top */
```

Or drop the `transform` when the card is not hovered.

## Why it works

A stacking context is a group that is painted as one unit; `z-index` values inside it are never compared with elements outside it. `transform` (other than `none`), `opacity` below 1, and positioned elements with a `z-index` all create one. Both cards sit at the same level, so the later card in the HTML paints over the earlier card, menu and all. `z-index` needs `position` (or a flex/grid item) to apply, hence `position: relative`.

## Verify it

Open a menu on the first card and confirm it covers the second card. In the DevTools Elements panel, walk up from the menu and check each ancestor's Computed `transform`, `opacity` and `z-index` to find the one that creates the stacking context.

cards.front: A phone-only checkout panel uses `height: 100vh` with the Pay button pinned at the bottom. On mobile browsers, the button is hidden behind the browser toolbar until the user scrolls. What should the height be?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Use the dynamic or small viewport unit instead of `vh`:

```css
.checkout {
  height: 100vh;   /* fallback for old browsers */
  height: 100dvh;  /* follows the toolbar as it shows and hides */
}
```

`100svh` (small viewport) also keeps the button visible, and does not resize while scrolling.

## Why it works

On mobile, `vh` is measured against the large viewport, the size when the address bar and toolbars are hidden. While they are visible the real visible area is shorter, so the bottom of a `100vh` box sits under them. `dvh` tracks the current visible height; `svh` uses the smallest (toolbars shown). The second `height` line overrides the first only in browsers that understand `dvh`.

## Verify it

Test on a real phone or a mobile emulator: load the page without scrolling and confirm the Pay button is fully visible. Scroll down and up and watch that it stays visible.

cards.front: A signup form has `<label for="email">Email</label>` and `<input name="email" type="email">`. Tapping the label does not focus the field, and a screen reader announces the input with no name. What is wrong?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

`for` must match the input's `id`, not its `name`. Add the id:

```html
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">
```

Or wrap the input inside the `<label>`, which needs no `for`/`id`.

## Why it works

`name` is the key sent to the server when the form submits; `id` identifies the element in the page. The label association uses `id`, and it gives the input its accessible name and makes a tap on the label focus the input, a bigger touch target on phones. With no matching id, the label is just nearby text.

## Verify it

Tap the label text and confirm the cursor moves into the field. In the console, `document.querySelector('label[for=email]').control` should return the input, not `null`. In DevTools, the Accessibility pane should show the input's name as "Email".

cards.front: An edit form shows the record's ID in `<input name="id" value="42" disabled>` so users cannot change it. The server says `id` is missing from the submitted form. Why, and what should you use instead?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Disabled controls are not submitted. Use `readonly` if the user should see the value:

```html
<input name="id" value="42" readonly>
```

If they need not see it, use `<input type="hidden" name="id" value="42">`. Better still, put the ID in the URL (`POST /tasks/42`) and have the server check the user may edit that record.

## Why it works

The HTML form rules skip disabled controls when building the submitted data, so `disabled` means "not part of this form right now". `readonly` blocks editing but the value is still submitted and the field can still be focused. Either way, the value is not trustworthy: anyone can change it with DevTools, so the server must authorize the ID it receives.

## Verify it

Submit the form and look at the request in the DevTools Network panel (Payload tab): `id=42` should be present. In the console, `[...new FormData(form)]` lists exactly what will be sent.

cards.front: A task form has `<input type="checkbox" name="done">`. Unchecking it and saving never marks the task as not done: the server keeps the old value. What does the browser send, and how should the server handle it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

An unchecked checkbox sends nothing at all, and a checked one sends `done=on`. The server must treat a missing field as `false`:

```python
done = "done" in request.form   # True if checked, False if absent
```

Don't write `if "done" in form: task.done = True`; that has no way to turn it off.

## Why it works

HTML submits a checkbox only when it is checked, with its `value` (default `"on"`). There is no "unchecked" value, so an update handler that only changes fields present in the request never sees the uncheck. For a full edit form, the checkbox's absence is the answer "false". A JavaScript client can instead send JSON with `done: checkbox.checked`, which is always a boolean.

## Verify it

Check and uncheck the box and compare the request payloads in the Network panel: `done=on` in one, no `done` key in the other. Write a server test that posts the form without `done` and asserts the task is saved as not done.

cards.front: An SPA's fetch wrapper sends users to /login on any 401 or 403. A signed-in viewer clicks Edit, gets 403, and is sent to the login page again and again. What should change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Handle the two codes differently. On **401** (no valid credentials, such as an expired session) send the user to login and return them afterwards. On **403** (known user, action not allowed) keep them on the page and show "You don't have permission to edit this task", and hide or disable Edit for viewers. The server should keep answering 403 here, not 401.

## Why it works

401 means "I don't know who you are": signing in can fix it, and the response must carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the scheme. 403 means "I know who you are, and no": signing in again produces the same identity and the same 403, which is why the user loops. Some APIs answer 404 instead of 403 to hide that a private record exists; then the client simply shows "not found".

## Verify it

With curl, `curl -i -X PUT localhost:3000/tasks/7` without a token should print `401 Unauthorized` and `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`; with a viewer's token it should print `403 Forbidden`. In the app, sign in as a viewer and force the edit: the page should show the permission message and the URL should not change to /login.

cards.front: A checkout endpoint answers form POSTs with `303 See Other` and `Location: /orders/81`. A new React page calls it with fetch, and `await res.json()` throws "Unexpected token '<'". Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

fetch followed the redirect by itself: it sent `GET /orders/81` and resolved with that HTML confirmation page (status 200, `res.redirected` true), so `res.json()` tried to parse HTML. The order was saved. Give script callers an API response instead, such as `POST /api/orders` returning `201 Created`, `Location: /orders/81` and the order as JSON, and keep the 303 for the plain HTML form.

## Why it works

fetch follows 3xx redirects automatically (the default `redirect: 'follow'`), and after a 303 the follow-up is a GET with no body. Your code only sees the final response, so it gets 200 from /orders/81, not the 303, and a body meant for a browser tab. Post/redirect/get fits full-page form submissions, where the browser should show the next page; a script needs data it can read.

## Verify it

Log `res.status, res.redirected, res.url` before parsing: before the fix it prints `200 true …/orders/81`, after it prints `201 false …/api/orders` and `res.json()` returns the order. In the DevTools Network panel the old flow shows the POST answered with 303, then a GET for /orders/81 returning HTML.

cards.front: Users rename a task, the PATCH returns 200, but reopening the list shows the old title for about an hour. `GET /api/tasks` sends `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`. Why, and what should it send?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The browser is reusing its stored copy of `GET /api/tasks` for up to an hour without asking the server, which `max-age=3600` allows. Send `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` with an `ETag`, or `no-store` if revalidating is not worth it. The browser then checks with the server on every load and gets a cheap 304 when nothing changed.

## Why it works

While a stored response is fresh (younger than max-age), a cache serves it with no network request at all. A successful unsafe request such as a PATCH does invalidate stored responses for its own URL, but this edit went to `/api/tasks/7`, a different URL, so the list copy stays. `private` keeps shared caches such as a CDN from serving one user's list to another.

## Verify it

In the DevTools Network panel, reload the list: before the fix the tasks request shows "(disk cache)" or "(memory cache)" in the Size column and nothing reaches the server log. After the fix a request appears every time — 304 when unchanged, 200 right after an edit. `curl -i` on the endpoint should show the new Cache-Control and an ETag.

cards.front: A React app on localhost:5173 fetches an API on localhost:3000 with `credentials: 'include'`. The API sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`; the console shows a CORS error, yet the server logged 200. What must it send?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Credentialed requests refuse the wildcard. Send the exact origin, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173`, together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and add `Vary: Origin` because the value depends on the request. Take allowed origins from an allowlist in config; never echo back any Origin with credentials enabled.

## Why it works

The server did handle the request, hence the 200 in its log. CORS is enforced by the browser, which then refuses to hand the response to JavaScript. When cookies or HTTP authentication are included, the rules require the allowed origin to match exactly and the credentials header to be `true`, so `*` fails. `Vary: Origin` stops a cache from serving one origin's header to another.

## Verify it

`curl -i -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' localhost:3000/api/tasks` should show both headers with the exact origin, and the same request with an unlisted Origin should get no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. In the browser, the console error disappears and the response headers in the Network panel list both values.

cards.front: A fetch wrapper saves each response's ETag and sends it back as `If-None-Match` on the next GET. Now it throws "Request failed: 304" and the list is blank. Why, and how should it handle this?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

A 304 has no body, and `response.ok` is false because it only covers 200–299, so `if (!res.ok) throw` fires. Once you send If-None-Match yourself you own the cache: on 304, return the data you saved with that ETag. The simpler option is to drop the manual header and let the browser's HTTP cache revalidate; fetch then hands you the stored 200 transparently.

## Why it works

When a browser revalidates its own cached copy, it adds If-None-Match itself and turns the 304 into the stored 200 before your code sees it. When your code adds a conditional header, fetch skips the HTTP cache for that request and passes the raw 304 through, because only your code knows which saved copy the tag refers to.

## Verify it

Unit-test the wrapper against a small node:http server that returns 200 with an ETag, then 304 when If-None-Match matches: assert both calls return the same data and nothing throws. In the DevTools Network panel the second request shows status 304 and a tiny transfer size.

cards.front: A mobile client retries `DELETE /tasks/7` after a timeout. The retry gets 404, and the app shows "Delete failed" even though the task is gone. How should the client treat this?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

When a DELETE is a retry, treat 404 as "already deleted": remove the row and show no error. The first attempt most likely succeeded and only its response was lost. Some APIs instead answer 204 for a record the caller already deleted, for example a soft-deleted row; either way, write the rule into the API contract so clients agree.

## Why it works

DELETE is idempotent: repeating it leaves the same server state — no task 7 — but the response can differ. The first attempt probably returned 204 before the network dropped it, and the repeat finds nothing to delete. Idempotency promises the same effect, not the same status code, so the client must read the second response in light of the retry.

## Verify it

Against a local server, run `curl -i -X DELETE localhost:3000/tasks/7` twice: the first prints `204 No Content`, the second `404 Not Found`. In a client test, make the first call time out and the second return 404, then assert that the row is removed and no error message appears.

cards.front: POST /tasks with a blank title returns 400 as expected, yet a blank task appears in the list and the server log shows "Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client". What is the bug?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The validation branch sends the 400 but does not stop the handler. Change `res.status(400).json(…)` to `return res.status(400).json(…)`. Execution then ends at the error response instead of falling through to the insert and the second `res.status(201).json(task)`.

## Why it works

Sending a response does not exit the function. The code after the `if` still runs: it saves the task, then tries to set a 201 status and headers on a response that has already been sent, so Node throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. The client already has the 400, which is why the bug looks like "validation works" while bad data is stored.

## Verify it

Send `curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"   "}'`, then GET /tasks: no new task should exist and the log should have no ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. Add a test that posts a blank title and asserts both the 400 and an unchanged task count.

cards.front: A React form POSTs with fetch and body: JSON.stringify({ title }), but sets no headers. The Express 5 API uses express.json(), yet every create fails with a 500 "Cannot destructure property 'title' of 'req.body'". Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The request has no `Content-Type: application/json` header, so `express.json()` ignores it and `req.body` stays `undefined`. Add `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }` to the `fetch` call. On the server, also check that the body is an object and return a 400 instead of crashing.

## Why it works

When `fetch` gets a string body and no content type, it sends `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`. `express.json()` parses only requests whose content type matches JSON; anything else passes through untouched. In Express 5 the untouched `req.body` is `undefined`, so `const { title } = req.body` throws, and Express turns the thrown error into a 500.

## Verify it

In DevTools, Network, select the request and look at Request Headers: `Content-Type` should read `application/json` after the fix. Repeat the create and confirm a 201 with the task in the response body.

cards.front: After adding a requireUser middleware, signed-out requests to GET /tasks get a 401 immediately, but signed-in requests spin forever with no error logged. What is likely missing?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The middleware never calls `next()` on the success path. After it sets `req.user`, add `next()` so Express moves on to the route handler. Keep `return res.status(401).json(…)` for the signed-out branch.

## Why it works

Express moves to the next function only when the current one calls `next()` (or `next(err)`). A middleware that neither responds nor calls `next` leaves the request open. Nothing throws, so no error handler or log fires; the request simply stays pending until the client times out.

## Verify it

Run `curl -i -m 5 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" localhost:3000/tasks`: before the fix it times out after 5 seconds, after the fix it returns 200. In DevTools the request should no longer show as "pending".

cards.front: After upgrading an app to Express 5, the server crashes at startup with "PathError: Missing parameter name at index 1: *" pointing at app.get('*', sendIndexHtml). What changed, and what is the fix?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Express 5 uses a newer path matcher where a bare `*` is not valid; a wildcard must be named. Use `app.get('/{*splat}', sendIndexHtml)` to match every path including `/`, or `'/*splat'` to match everything except the root. Optional params changed too: `/tasks/:id?` becomes `/tasks{/:id}`.

## Why it works

Express 5 moved to path-to-regexp v8, which rejects unnamed wildcards and the `?` suffix at the moment the route is registered, so the error appears at startup rather than on a request. The matched segments arrive as an array in `req.params.splat`, for example `['tasks', '5']` for /tasks/5.

## Verify it

Start the server and confirm it boots. Then request `/` and a deep URL such as `/tasks/5` and check both return the SPA HTML with 200, while API routes registered earlier still return JSON.

cards.front: A developer sets SEND_EMAILS=false in .env to stop emails locally, runs node --env-file=.env server.js, and the code checks if (process.env.SEND_EMAILS). Emails still send. Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Environment values are strings, and `"false"` is a non-empty string, so it is truthy. Compare explicitly: `const sendEmails = process.env.SEND_EMAILS === 'true'`. Parse the flag once in a config module so every caller gets a real boolean.

## Why it works

`--env-file` copies the text after `=` into `process.env` without type conversion. JavaScript treats every non-empty string as truthy, including `"false"` and `"0"`. Only a missing variable (`undefined`) or an empty value would be falsy, which is fragile to rely on.

## Verify it

Run `node --env-file=.env -e "console.log(JSON.stringify(process.env.SEND_EMAILS))"` to see `"false"`. After the fix, log the parsed `sendEmails` at startup and confirm it prints `false`, then trigger a flow that sends email and check nothing goes out.

cards.front: An Express 5 API has a custom JSON error handler, yet a failing GET /tasks/1 returns an HTML page showing the stack trace. The handler is registered right after express.json(), above the routes. Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Error handlers only receive errors raised earlier in the stack, so one registered above the routes never sees their errors. Move the four-argument handler to the very end, after all routes and the 404 catch-all. Failures then return your JSON body with a 500.

## Why it works

Express passes an error forward from the point where it happened, skipping ordinary middleware and looking for the next error handler below it. With none below the routes, the built-in handler replies with an HTML page; in development it includes the stack trace, and in production (`NODE_ENV=production`) it shows only "Internal Server Error".

## Verify it

Make a route throw on purpose and run `curl -i localhost:3000/tasks/1`: the response should be `Content-Type: application/json` with your error body, not HTML. Remove the test throw afterwards.

cards.front: A session expires while a user edits /notes/7. Their next save gets 401, the SPA sends them to /login, and after signing in they land on the home page. How should the app return them to /notes/7 safely?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

On 401, navigate to `/login?returnTo=` plus `encodeURIComponent(location.pathname + location.search)`. After a successful login, parse `returnTo` with `new URL(value, location.origin)` and redirect to `url.pathname + url.search + url.hash` only when `url.origin === location.origin`; otherwise go to `/`. Keep the unsaved draft (for example in sessionStorage) so the edit survives the round trip.

## Why it works

The query parameter carries the destination through the login page, and encoding stops `?tab=edit` being read as the login page's own query. Validation matters because `returnTo` is attacker-controlled: `/login?returnTo=//evil.example` would make your real login page forward a freshly signed-in user to a phishing site (an open redirect). A plain `startsWith('/')` check is not enough: `//evil.example` starts with `/` but resolves to the host evil.example, as Node 22's URL parser confirmed.

## Verify it

Unit-test the validator: `/notes/7?tab=edit` is kept, while `https://evil.example/login`, `//evil.example`, `/\evil.example`, and `javascript:alert(1)` all become `/`. Then delete the session cookie in DevTools, save a note, sign in, and confirm the address bar returns to /notes/7.

cards.front: In development the React app runs on localhost:5173 and the Express API on localhost:3000. POST /login returns 204 with a Set-Cookie header, but the next GET /me still returns 401. What is wrong?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The calls are cross-origin (different port), and fetch's default `credentials: 'same-origin'` neither stores the login cookie nor sends it. Simplest fix: proxy `/api` through the Vite dev server (`server.proxy`) so the browser sees one origin. Otherwise pass `credentials: 'include'` on every call and have the API reply with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173` (not `*`) and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

## Why it works

An origin is scheme + host + port, so the two ports are different origins. Per MDN, `credentials` controls both whether cookies are sent and whether `Set-Cookie` in the response is respected, and a cross-origin request with `include` only succeeds if the server opts in with Allow-Credentials and an exact origin. SameSite is not the culprit: ports don't change the site, so both are same-site. A proxy avoids CORS entirely and matches production, where app and API usually share a domain.

## Verify it

In the DevTools Network panel, confirm the failing GET /me request has no `Cookie` request header. After the fix, the same request carries `Cookie: sid=…` and returns 200, and a page reload keeps you signed in.

cards.front: Login returns the same 'Invalid email or password' text and status for every failure, yet a tester can tell which emails have accounts by timing the responses. What leaks, and how do you fix it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The handler returns immediately when the email is unknown but runs the slow password hash when it exists, so response time reveals which accounts exist. Make both paths do the same work: when no user matches, verify the submitted password against a fixed dummy hash, then return the same 401 and message. Add per-account and per-IP throttling so probing cannot scale.

## Why it works

Password hashing is deliberately slow; that is its job. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet describes this exact discrepancy: an early return for unknown users is much faster than the hash-and-compare path, even with identical text and status. On the test machine (Node 22, scrypt), the leaky handler averaged about 819 ms for a real account and 0.01 ms for an unknown one; with a dummy hash both took over 500 ms. Headers and redirects must match too.

## Verify it

Write a script that times 20 failed logins for a known email and 20 for an unknown one and compares the averages; they should be close. Also diff the two responses' status, headers, and body: nothing but timing noise should differ.

cards.front: After each deploy every user is logged out, and on the two-instance production setup users are randomly bounced to /login between clicks. The app uses express-session with default settings. What is wrong?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

express-session's default MemoryStore keeps sessions in one process's memory. A restart wipes them, and each instance has its own copy, so a request routed to the other instance finds no session. Configure a shared, persistent store (a Redis or PostgreSQL session store package) used by every instance, and give all instances the same `secret`.

## Why it works

The cookie holds only the session ID; the data lives in the store. With MemoryStore, instance A creates the session and instance B has never seen that ID, so the user looks anonymous. express-session warns about this: with `NODE_ENV=production` it printed "MemoryStore is not designed for a production environment, as it will leak memory, and will not scale past a single process." Sticky load balancing hides the random bounces but still loses every session on restart.

## Verify it

Log in, restart the server (or route the next request to the other instance), and call `GET /me`: it should still return 200. Check startup logs for the MemoryStore warning, and look in the store for the session record (with connect-redis, keys start with `sess:`).

cards.front: Login works locally, but in production behind an HTTPS load balancer the POST /login response has no Set-Cookie header at all. The app uses express-session with `cookie: { secure: true }`. Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

TLS ends at the load balancer, so the Node app receives plain HTTP, and express-session refuses to set a `secure` cookie on what looks like an insecure request. Add `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` (one proxy hop) so Express trusts the load balancer's `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` and `req.secure` becomes true.

## Why it works

express-session only sends a Secure cookie when `req.secure` is true. Without trust proxy, Express ignores `X-Forwarded-*` headers, because clients could forge them. In an Express 5.2 and express-session 1.19 test, a login request with `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` got no Set-Cookie without trust proxy, and `sid=…; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` with it. Use the real hop count rather than `true`, which trusts every forwarded value a client sends.

## Verify it

Log `req.secure` and `req.protocol` for one request in production; they should be `true` and `https`. Then check the login response in the DevTools Network panel: it should include a Set-Cookie with `Secure`, and `GET /me` should return 200.

cards.front: The server keeps sessions for 30 days, yet desktop users must log in again every time they reopen the browser. The login Set-Cookie header has no Expires or Max-Age. What is happening?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Without Expires or Max-Age the cookie is a session cookie, which the browser may delete when it closes, orphaning the server's 30-day record. For a "Remember me" checkbox, give the cookie a lifetime only when it is ticked: in express-session, set `req.session.cookie.maxAge = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000` after regenerating the session at login, and keep the store's expiry in line.

## Why it works

express-session sends no Expires by default. Setting maxAge in the test changed the header to `sid=…; Path=/; Expires=Sat, 24 Oct 2026 …; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`, 30 days out. MDN notes that browser session-restore can keep session cookies alive, which is why some users never notice. OWASP prefers non-persistent session cookies, so make persistence an explicit user choice and still enforce expiry on the server.

## Verify it

Log in with and without "Remember me" and compare the Set-Cookie headers in the DevTools Network panel: only the remembered login carries Expires, and the Application panel's cookie list shows "Session" for the other. Fully quit and reopen the browser to confirm.

cards.front: A spending report runs SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, total_cents FROM orders, expecting one row per customer, but customer 1 appears twice. Why, and what query gives one row per customer with a total?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Group and aggregate instead: `SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_cents) AS spent_cents, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;` It returns exactly one row per customer; in the test data, customer 1 got 3500 over 2 orders and customer 2 got 1400 over 2 orders.

## Why it works

DISTINCT removes rows that are identical in every selected column. Customer 1's orders total 1000 and 2500, so (1, 1000) and (1, 2500) are different rows and both stay. Customer 2's two orders were both 700, so DISTINCT merged them into one row, and any sum over that result would undercount. GROUP BY makes one group per customer_id and lets SUM and COUNT combine the rows inside each group. Use DISTINCT to de-duplicate a list; use GROUP BY when you need one row per something plus a calculation.

## Verify it

Seed a customer with two orders of the same amount and run both queries: DISTINCT shows one row for them, while GROUP BY shows the doubled total and a count of 2. Then check the report has as many rows as SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders returns.

cards.front: A migration runs ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN plan text NOT NULL on a production table that already has rows, and PostgreSQL rejects it. What should the migration do instead?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

If every existing user should get the same value, add a default in the same statement: `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN plan text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free';`. If the value depends on other data, add the column as nullable, backfill it with an UPDATE, and then run `ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN plan SET NOT NULL` (PostgreSQL syntax; SQLite cannot alter a column's constraints this way).

## Why it works

Existing rows have no value for the new column, so they would hold NULL, which breaks NOT NULL, and the whole statement fails. With a constant DEFAULT, PostgreSQL stores that value in the table's metadata instead of rewriting every row, so the change stays quick on a large table, and later inserts that omit plan get it too. SET NOT NULL succeeds only when no row holds NULL, and PostgreSQL scans the table to check, so run it after the backfill and after the app writes the column on every insert.

## Verify it

On a staging copy, run the migration and confirm SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE plan IS NULL returns 0. Insert a user without a plan and confirm it reads back 'free'. For the backfill route, compare the UPDATE's affected-row count with the number of existing rows before running SET NOT NULL.

cards.front: A newsletter signup runs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email, list) DO NOTHING, but PostgreSQL rejects it on every call. The subscriptions table has only an id primary key. What is missing?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

A unique constraint (or unique index) on exactly those columns: `ALTER TABLE subscriptions ADD CONSTRAINT subscriptions_email_list_key UNIQUE (email, list);`. After that, the same INSERT runs, and repeating it for the same email and list inserts nothing.

## Why it works

ON CONFLICT (email, list) does not search for duplicates by itself. PostgreSQL uses the column list to infer which unique index defines a conflict, and when no unique index matches, inference fails and the statement raises an error instead of running. SQLite behaves the same way, reporting that the ON CONFLICT clause does not match any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint. Creating the constraint fails if duplicate pairs already exist, so find and clean those up first.

## Verify it

Before adding the constraint, find existing duplicates with SELECT email, list, COUNT(*) FROM subscriptions GROUP BY email, list HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Then, on staging, add it, run the signup INSERT twice for the same pair, and confirm neither call errors and SELECT count(*) for that pair returns 1.

cards.front: A task list filters by tag with JOIN task_tags, JOIN tags, and WHERE tags.name IN ('bug', 'urgent'). A task that has both tags appears twice. How should the query be written?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Keep tasks as the only table in the outer FROM and move the tag test into EXISTS: `SELECT t.id, t.title FROM tasks t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM task_tags tt JOIN tags g ON g.id = tt.tag_id WHERE tt.task_id = t.id AND g.name IN ('bug', 'urgent'));` Each task now appears once, however many of the chosen tags it has.

## Why it works

The JOIN produces one row per matching (task, tag) pair. A task tagged both 'bug' and 'urgent' yields two rows, and LIMIT/OFFSET pagination counts it twice as well, so pages show fewer distinct tasks than expected. EXISTS only asks whether at least one matching tag row exists, so it cannot multiply the task. DISTINCT would also hide the duplicates, but EXISTS states the intent and keeps working when you select more columns.

## Verify it

Seed one task with both tags and one with a single tag, then assert that the endpoint returns 2 tasks. In a SQLite run of this data, the JOIN version returned task ids 1, 1, 3 and the EXISTS version returned 1, 3.

cards.front: Search passes local tests on SQLite, but in production PostgreSQL typing 'invoice' no longer finds 'Invoice March'. The query is title LIKE '%' || $1 || '%'. What changed, and how do you fix it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

In PostgreSQL, LIKE is case-sensitive, while SQLite's LIKE ignores case for ASCII letters by default. For a case-insensitive search in PostgreSQL, use `title ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'` (ILIKE is a PostgreSQL extension, not standard SQL), or `lower(title) LIKE '%' || lower($1) || '%'`, which behaves the same in both databases for ASCII text (SQLite's `lower()` folds only ASCII letters).

## Why it works

The same SQL text behaved differently because the two databases define LIKE differently. PostgreSQL's docs describe ILIKE as matching case-insensitively according to the active locale. Turning on SQLite's PRAGMA case_sensitive_like, which mimics PostgreSQL, made the local query stop finding 'Invoice March' too, reproducing the production bug. On a large table, a plain index on title does not speed up a '%term%' search in either form.

## Verify it

Add a test with mixed-case data ('Invoice March') and a lowercase search term, and run it against PostgreSQL, the database production uses, not only SQLite. Confirm the fixed query returns the row, and that an unrelated title such as 'Receipt' is still excluded.

cards.front: A one-off script meant to close task 42 ran UPDATE tasks SET done = true with its WHERE clause missing, and every task is now done. How could the script have caught this before it became permanent?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Run manual data fixes inside a transaction and check the affected-row count before committing: `BEGIN;` then `UPDATE tasks SET done = true WHERE id = 42;`, which psql reports as `UPDATE 1`, then `COMMIT` only if the count is what you expected, otherwise `ROLLBACK`. In a script, read rowCount and roll back automatically when it differs.

## Why it works

Until COMMIT, a transaction's changes are not permanent and ROLLBACK discards them. The affected-row count is the cheapest sanity check: in a test run on a 500-row table, the statement without WHERE reported 500 rows, the rollback left 0 tasks done, and the corrected statement reported 1. Adding `RETURNING id` shows exactly which rows changed. After COMMIT, recovery means restoring a backup or writing a reverse UPDATE by hand.

## Verify it

Rehearse on a staging copy: run the script with the WHERE clause deliberately removed and confirm it prints the unexpected count, rolls back, and SELECT count(*) FROM tasks WHERE done shows no change. Then run the correct version and confirm it reports exactly 1 row.

cards.front: A React 19 create form uses `useActionState`, and its Add button is never disabled. A user double-clicks Add during a slow save, and two identical tasks appear. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Disable the button while the action runs: `<button disabled={isPending}>` using the third value from `useActionState` (or `pending` from `useFormStatus` in a child button component). For creates that must happen only once even across network retries, also send an idempotency key that the server checks.

## Why it works

React does not drop the second submit. Calls to a `useActionState` action are queued and run one after another: the second waits for the first to finish, receives its returned state as `previousState`, and then runs with its own FormData, which still holds the same title. The server therefore receives two POSTs. A disabled submit button cannot start another submission, so only one action is queued.

## Verify it

In a component test, click Add twice before the mocked API resolves and assert the mock was called once. In the browser, throttle the network in DevTools, double-click Add, and confirm the Network panel shows a single `POST /api/tasks`.

cards.front: A signup form moved to React 19 `<form action={formAction}>` with `useActionState`. Now a server validation error ("Email already used") also wipes every field the user typed. Why, and how do you keep the values?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Return the submitted values in the action's state and feed them back as default values: `return { error: 'Email already used', values: { email } }` and `<input name="email" defaultValue={state.values?.email} />`. Alternatively, keep `onSubmit` with `e.preventDefault()` for this form, which never triggers the automatic reset.

## Why it works

When a function passed to a form's `action` finishes without throwing, React resets the form's uncontrolled fields. Returning an error object is still a normal finish, so the reset happens. Reset puts each field back to its default value; pointing `defaultValue` at the last submitted value makes the reset restore what the user typed, while a successful save returns empty values and clears the form.

## Verify it

Submit an invalid value and confirm the error appears and the field still shows the value; then submit a valid value and confirm the form clears. A Testing Library test can assert on `input.value` after the action resolves.

cards.front: A checkout confirmation step sends `POST /api/orders` from a `useEffect` when it mounts. In local development every checkout creates two orders; production creates one. What is happening, and where should the POST live?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Move the POST into the handler of the user action that causes it, the Place order button's submit or click handler, and let the effect only read data. Do not remove StrictMode or add a "ran once" ref to hide the duplicate.

## Why it works

StrictMode in development mounts the component, runs its effects, cleans them up, and runs them again, to check that effects are safe to repeat. Effects are for keeping a component in sync with something outside React while it is shown; creating an order is a one-time consequence of a click and cannot be undone by a cleanup. The development double run exposes the same bug users would hit in production whenever the step remounts, for example after navigating back.

## Verify it

With StrictMode on in development, open the confirmation step and confirm the Network panel shows no `POST /api/orders` until you click. One click should produce exactly one POST and one new row in the orders table.

cards.front: After a successful save on `/tasks/new`, the app calls `navigate('/tasks/' + created.id)`. Pressing Back shows the create form again, and users save duplicates. Which React Router option fixes the history?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Navigate with `replace`: `navigate('/tasks/' + created.id, { replace: true })`. The new task page replaces the `/tasks/new` history entry, so Back returns to the task list instead of the create form.

## Why it works

`navigate(to)` pushes a new history entry by default, so the stack becomes `/tasks`, `/tasks/new`, `/tasks/42` and Back lands on the form. With `{ replace: true }` React Router swaps the current entry, leaving `/tasks`, `/tasks/42`. It is the client-side version of redirecting after a successful form post, which keeps a finished form out of the back history.

## Verify it

In a test, render a `MemoryRouter` with `initialEntries={['/tasks', '/tasks/new']}` and `initialIndex={1}`, save, then call `navigate(-1)` and assert the location is `/tasks`. By hand: save a task, press Back, and confirm you see the list.

cards.front: An edit-task form saves `done: formData.get('done') === 'true'` from `<input type="checkbox" name="done" />`. Checking the box and saving always stores `done: false`. Why, and what is the correct read?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Read presence instead of a made-up value: `done: formData.has('done')`, or compare with `'on'`, the value a checkbox without a `value` attribute submits. If the input sets `value="true"`, comparing with `'true'` would also work.

## Why it works

FormData follows HTML form submission rules. A checked checkbox contributes its `value`, which defaults to the string `'on'`; an unchecked checkbox is left out, so `get('done')` returns `null`. Every FormData value is a string (or a File), never a boolean, so the code must compare against what the browser actually sends.

## Verify it

Log `Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form))` with the box checked and unchecked: you will see `{ done: 'on', … }` and no `done` key at all. Add a test that saves both states and asserts `true` and `false` reach the API.

cards.front: A task list builds `const filters = { status }` in render and runs `useEffect(() => { fetchTasks(filters).then(setTasks); }, [filters])`. `/api/tasks` is requested over and over. Why, and what should it depend on?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Depend on the primitive value, not on an object rebuilt every render: create the filters inside the effect and list `[status]` as the dependency. If the object must be shared with other code, memoize it with `useMemo(() => ({ status }), [status])`.

## Why it works

React compares each dependency with `Object.is`. A new `{ status }` object is created on every render, so it never equals the previous one and the effect runs after every render. Each response calls `setTasks` with a new array, which re-renders, which creates another object, which runs the effect again: a request loop. The string `'open'` is equal from one render to the next, so the effect runs only when the status changes.

## Verify it

After the fix, loading the page sends one request and changing the status filter sends one more. In a test, mock `fetch`, render the list, wait for it to settle, and assert the mock was called once.

cards.front: An API test file has 'lists tasks' expecting 2 rows. It passes with it.only, but in the full file it sees 3, because an earlier test inserted a task. How do you fix it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Give every test a clean database. In `beforeEach`, either create a fresh test database (for example an in-memory SQLite one), delete all rows from the tables, or start a transaction and roll it back in `afterEach`. Then each test inserts exactly the rows it asserts on. Never point tests at your development database.

## Why it works

Tests in one file share whatever the database holds, and Vitest runs them in order by default. Rows left by one test become hidden input to the next, so results depend on which tests ran first. `it.only` hides the problem because the earlier test never runs. A rolled-back transaction is fast because nothing is committed, but it only works when the code under test uses that same connection.

## Verify it

Run the file with `npx vitest run --sequence.shuffle` a few times; order-dependent tests fail at random until the reset is in place. Also run each test alone with `-t "lists tasks"` and confirm the result matches the full run.

cards.front: The Task type gains a required priority field, and tsc now reports errors in 40 tests that build task objects by hand. How can test data be set up so the next new field is a one-line change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Add a test data builder and use it in every test:

```ts
let nextId = 1
export function buildTask(overrides: Partial<Task> = {}): Task {
  return { id: nextId++, title: 'Buy milk', done: false, priority: 'normal', ...overrides }
}
```

Tests pass only the fields they care about, such as `buildTask({ done: true })`. The next required field is added once, in the builder.

## Why it works

Hand-written objects repeat every field in every test, so each schema change touches all of them. The builder keeps valid defaults in one place, and the spread lets each test override only what matters, which also makes the test's intent obvious. A counter for `id` keeps built records distinct, so tests that insert several rows do not collide on the key.

## Verify it

Add a new required field to `Task`, update only `buildTask`, and run `npx tsc --noEmit`: it should report no errors in the tests. Read one test and confirm the fields it passes are exactly the ones its assertions depend on.

cards.front: A validateTitle test file has six near-identical tests for an empty title, a blank title, 81 characters, and so on. A reviewer asks you to collapse them and keep readable failure names. What do you write?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Put the cases in a table and let `it.each` generate one test per row:

```ts
it.each([
  { case: 'empty', title: '', error: 'Title is required' },
  { case: 'blank', title: '   ', error: 'Title is required' },
  { case: '81-char', title: 'x'.repeat(81), error: 'Title is too long' },
])('rejects $case title', ({ title, error }) => {
  expect(validateTitle(title)).toBe(error)
})
```

Keep the accepted values (1 and 80 characters) in a second table.

## Why it works

`it.each` generates one test per row, so each case still passes or fails on its own. With object rows, `$case` in the name is replaced by that row's value, giving names such as `rejects 'blank' title`. A short `case` label reads better than printing the 81-character title itself. Splitting rejected and accepted cases keeps each assertion simple instead of branching inside the test.

## Verify it

Run `npx vitest run validateTitle` and confirm the report lists one named test per row. Break one expected message on purpose and check that only that row fails, with its label in the failure name.

cards.front: A test file defines const sendEmail = vi.fn() at the top. The second test asserts toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) but gets 2, because the first test also called it. What should the file do?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Clear mock history before each test: `beforeEach(() => vi.clearAllMocks())`, or set `clearMocks: true` in the Vitest config. Alternatively, create the mock inside each test so nothing is shared.

## Why it works

A mock's `.mock.calls` list lives as long as the mock object. A file-level `vi.fn()` is shared by every test in the file, so calls pile up. `clearAllMocks` empties the recorded calls but keeps any `mockReturnValue` you set; `vi.resetAllMocks` also resets implementations. `vi.restoreAllMocks` only puts back methods replaced by `vi.spyOn`; since Vitest 3 it does not clear a `vi.fn()`'s calls. Pick the lightest one that makes each test start clean.

## Verify it

Run the file with `--sequence.shuffle` and then each test alone with `-t`. Both should pass. Temporarily delete the `beforeEach` and confirm the count assertion fails again, which proves the clearing is what fixed it.

cards.front: A task list test calls screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }) and fails with 'Found multiple elements with the role "button" and name "Delete"'. How do you click the Delete for 'Pay rent'?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Scope the query to that row with `within`: `const row = screen.getByText('Pay rent').closest('li')!` then `await user.click(within(row).getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }))`. Even better, give each button a specific name, such as `aria-label={'Delete ' + task.title}`, and query `getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete Pay rent' })`.

## Why it works

`getBy…` queries require exactly one match; several matches throw, so a test cannot click the wrong row by accident. `within(element)` runs the same queries inside one part of the page. A per-row accessible name helps real users too: a screen reader user tabbing through the list otherwise hears "Delete, Delete, Delete" with no hint of which task each one removes.

## Verify it

After the click, assert `expect(screen.queryByText('Pay rent')).not.toBeInTheDocument()` and `expect(screen.getByText('Buy milk')).toBeInTheDocument()`, so the test proves the right row was removed and its neighbour survived.

cards.front: A test asserts create was called with { title: 'Buy milk' }, but the code also sends createdAt: new Date().toISOString(), so the assertion fails. How do you check the title without hard-coding a timestamp?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Use asymmetric matchers: `expect(create).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ title: 'Buy milk', createdAt: expect.any(String) }))`. If the exact timestamp matters, pin the clock instead: `vi.useFakeTimers()` plus `vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-01-31T12:00:00Z'))`, then expect `createdAt: '2026-01-31T12:00:00.000Z'`.

## Why it works

`toHaveBeenCalledWith` compares arguments with deep equality, so an extra field makes it fail. `expect.objectContaining` matches when the listed fields are present and equal, and `expect.any(String)` accepts any string. That keeps the test about what it cares about, the title, while still checking that a timestamp was sent. Pinning the clock makes the value predictable when the format itself is the requirement.

## Verify it

Temporarily change the code to send `title: 'Buy mil'` and confirm the test fails; then remove `createdAt` from the payload and confirm `expect.any(String)` fails too. Restore the code and see it pass.

cards.front: A page on localhost:5173 calls fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/tasks'). The catch block logs "TypeError: Failed to fetch", yet the API log shows the request arrived. What do you check?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Treat it as a CORS failure, not a network outage. In the Network panel the row's Status shows CORS error, and the Console names the missing header. Fix the API to send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173 (and answer the OPTIONS preflight for JSON requests), or proxy /api through the Vite dev server so the page and API share one origin.

## Why it works

The browser sent the request and the server answered, but the response did not grant this origin permission, so the browser refused to hand it to page JavaScript. fetch reports that as a generic TypeError and hides the status and body on purpose; only DevTools shows the real reason. That is why the server log and the error disagree.

## Verify it

Reload with the Network panel open after the fix: the row should show 200 instead of CORS error, and its response headers should include Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your page's origin. For a JSON POST, an OPTIONS preflight row should appear just before it.

cards.front: Users on mobile data report duplicate tasks after tapping Save, but on localhost you never see it. How do you reproduce it with DevTools?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Throttle the Network panel to a slow preset such as Slow 4G or 3G, clear the request list, and tap Save twice quickly. Two POST /api/tasks rows confirm the bug. Then disable the button while the request is pending and make the server safe to retry, for example with an idempotency key.

## Why it works

On localhost the POST finishes in milliseconds, so the first request is done before a second tap can land. Throttling stretches the request to phone-like timing, which opens the window between tap and response where a second tap sends a second POST. Duplicate taps are a timing bug, so you need slow timing to see it.

## Verify it

With throttling still on, tap Save repeatedly: the Network panel should show exactly one POST, and the button should stay disabled until the response arrives. Turn throttling off afterwards; the Network tab shows a warning icon while it is enabled.

cards.front: A settings page shows only "Something went wrong", and the Console is empty because the code catches every error. How can DevTools stop at the real error?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

In the Sources panel's Breakpoints pane, turn on pausing on caught exceptions and repeat the action. DevTools pauses on the line that throws, even though a try/catch handles it, so you can read the error, local values and the Call Stack. Then change the catch block to log or report the actual error instead of swallowing it.

## Why it works

A catch that only shows a generic message removes the error from the Console, so there is nothing to click. Exception breakpoints pause where the error is thrown, before the catch runs; caught and uncaught pausing are separate options and also cover rejected promises. Libraries sometimes throw and catch internally, so expect a few extra pauses you can skip.

## Verify it

With caught-exception pausing on, repeat the action: DevTools should stop on the throwing line with the error shown. After the catch calls console.error(error), the next failure should appear in the Console with its stack trace, and you can turn caught-exception pausing off again.

cards.front: Login returns 200 and sets a session cookie, but the next GET /api/tasks returns 401. How do you find out why the cookie is not being sent?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Open the GET /api/tasks request's Cookies tab in the Network panel and the cookie table in the Application panel. If the cookie exists but is not sent, compare its Domain, Path, SameSite and Secure values with the request. A common cause is Path=/api/auth set by the login route, which limits the cookie to /api/auth/*. Set Path=/ when creating the session cookie.

## Why it works

The browser attaches a cookie only when the request matches its domain, path prefix, Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite rules. For example, a cookie set with Path=/api/auth is sent to /api/auth/me but not to /api/tasks. If the browser refused to store a cookie at all, the Network panel marks the blocked response cookie and gives the reason in a tooltip.

## Verify it

After changing the cookie to Path=/, delete the old cookie in the Application panel and log in again. The GET /api/tasks request's Cookies tab should list sid, its request headers should include a Cookie header, and the response should be 200.

cards.front: After you change your app's IndexedDB schema, the dev build crashes on startup while reading data saved by the old version. How do you reset only this site's storage?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Use the Application panel's Storage view and clear site data for this origin. In one step it deletes IndexedDB, local storage, cookies and Cache Storage and unregisters the service worker, without touching other sites. Reload to start as a new user. Users will not do this for you, so still write an upgrade path for the old data.

## Why it works

The stored records match the old schema, so the new code reads fields that do not exist. Deleting each store by hand is error-prone; clearing site data resets every storage layer and also removes a service worker that might keep serving code for the old schema. Clearing only hides the bug on your machine; the fix is a migration, such as an IndexedDB onupgradeneeded handler or a new Dexie version().

## Verify it

After clearing, the Application panel should list no IndexedDB databases and no service worker for the origin, and the app should start like a first visit. To test the real fix, create data with the previous build, load the new build, and confirm it upgrades without crashing.

cards.front: In development, the Network panel shows GET /api/tasks twice on every page load. How do you find which code sends each one, and is it a bug?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Hover the Initiator column of each row to see the stack trace that sent it, and compare the two. If both come from the same useEffect in a React app running under StrictMode, it is expected in development: React runs effects an extra time to expose missing cleanup. If they come from different components, you have a real duplicate fetch to remove.

## Why it works

The Initiator column links a script-sent request to the line that sent it, and hovering shows the full call stack, so you can tell "same code twice" from "two callers". StrictMode's extra effect run happens only in development, so a production build should send one request. The effect should still abort or ignore the first request in its cleanup.

## Verify it

Build and preview the production app, then reload with the Network panel filtered to Fetch/XHR: there should be one GET /api/tasks. In development, both rows should show the same Initiator line; if they do not, find and remove the second caller.

cards.front: You rebased your PR branch onto `main` and ran `git push --force-with-lease`. It is rejected with "(stale info)". A teammate pushed a fix to your branch earlier. What do you do?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Do not switch to `--force`: that would delete your teammate's commit from the branch. Fetch, rebuild your branch from what is on GitHub (which includes their commit), rebase again, then push with the lease:

```bash
git branch feature-backup      # keep your rebased copy, just in case
git fetch
git reset --hard origin/feature  # your pushed work + their fix
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease
```

If you had commits you never pushed, cherry-pick them from `feature-backup`.

## Why it works

`--force-with-lease` only overwrites the remote branch if it still points where your remote-tracking ref `origin/feature` says. Your teammate's push moved it and you had not fetched since, so Git refused: exactly the protection you wanted. Plain `--force` skips that check. Careful: `git fetch` updates `origin/feature`, so after fetching, a lease push would succeed and overwrite their commit. Include their commit before pushing again.

## Verify it

Before pushing, `git log --oneline -5` should show the teammate's commit on your branch. In a scratch repo with two clones, the first lease push was rejected with "(stale info)"; after reset + rebase the push went through as a forced update and kept the teammate's commit. On GitHub, the PR's commit list should still include it.

cards.front: You changed `VITE_API_URL` in your static host's environment settings to point at the new API domain. The live Vite site still calls the old domain. Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The value was baked into the JavaScript when the site was built, so changing the setting afterwards does nothing. Trigger a new build and deploy with the new variable available to the build step. If the app is a PWA, the old service worker may keep serving cached files until the new version activates, so reload after it updates.

## Why it works

Vite statically replaces `import.meta.env.VITE_*` at build time: the built file contains the literal string, not a lookup. Environment settings only matter while `vite build` runs. In a scratch Vite 8 build, a bundle built without the variable contained `void 0`, and one built with `VITE_API_URL=https://prod.example.com` contained that exact string.

## Verify it

Fetch the deployed main bundle and search it for the domains, e.g. `curl -s https://app.example.com/assets/index-XXXX.js | grep -o "new-api.example.com"`. The new domain should appear and the old one should not. Then confirm in the DevTools Network panel that API requests go to the new host.

cards.front: CI fails at `npm ci`: "can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json … are in sync". You bumped a version in package.json by hand. What is the fix?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Run `npm install` locally so npm updates `package-lock.json` to match package.json, look at the lockfile diff, and commit it with package.json. Do not change CI to `npm install` to make the error go away.

## Why it works

`npm ci` installs only what the lockfile records, refuses to fix a mismatch, and never writes the lockfile. Your hand edit changed package.json but not the lock, so the lock is missing the new version. Local runs still worked because they used whatever was already in your `node_modules`; `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` and starts from the lockfile alone.

## Verify it

After `npm install`, `git status` should show `package-lock.json` modified along with package.json. Running `npm ci` locally should then finish without the sync error (in a scratch project, a hand-added `"dayjs": "1.11.13"` made it fail with "Missing: dayjs@1.11.13 from lock file"; after `npm install` it passed). The next CI run's install step should pass.

cards.front: Right after a deploy, some users of your Vite SPA get a blank screen and a console error saying a module script was served with MIME type "text/html". A reload fixes it. What happened?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Their open tab still asks for the previous build's hashed chunk (say `/assets/Settings-abc123.js`), which the new deploy removed. Your catch-all SPA rewrite answers that missing file with `index.html`, and the browser refuses to run HTML as a module. Keep the previous build's assets available for a while, make missing `/assets/*` return 404, and reload once when a lazy import fails (Vite fires a `vite:preloadError` event for this).

## Why it works

Build tools put a content hash in chunk names, so every deploy creates new file names. A lazily loaded route fetches its chunk only when first opened, possibly long after the page loaded. A fallback meant for page URLs like `/notes/42` also catches missing JS files unless it is limited to page routes. Module scripts require a JavaScript MIME type, so the HTML reply fails instead of giving a clear 404.

## Verify it

`curl -I https://your-site/assets/does-not-exist.js` should return 404, not 200 with `text/html`. In a scratch Node server, a catch-all fallback returned 200 text/html for `/assets/index-OLD123.js`, while a fallback limited to extension-less paths returned 404. Then rehearse: open the site, deploy, and open a lazy route in the old tab.

cards.front: Your PR from `feature/tasks` was squash-merged. You kept committing on the same branch and opened a new PR. It lists the old commits again and conflicts with `main`. What went wrong?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Squash-merging put one new commit on `main`; your branch's original commits never became part of `main`'s history, so Git still treats them as unmerged. Start a new branch from the updated `main` and move only the new work:

```bash
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c feature/tasks-2
git cherry-pick <new-commit-sha>
```

## Why it works

A PR shows the commits reachable from its branch but not from `main`. After a squash merge the old commits are still in that set. If `main` changed the same lines afterwards, Git has to merge those old commits against newer code, which produces conflicts you already solved once. GitHub's merge docs warn about exactly this and suggest a merge commit or a rebase for branches you keep working on.

## Verify it

`git log --oneline main..feature/tasks-2` should list only your new commits. In a scratch repo, the reused branch listed the already-squashed "validate title" commit and conflicted when merged; the fresh branch listed only the new "add extra" commit. The new PR on GitHub should show just those commits.

cards.front: The deploy job for your notes app just went green, and you are about to post "shipped" in the team channel. What should a two-minute smoke check on production cover?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

On the real production URL: (1) the site loads and shows the new version (the changed screen, or a version or commit label if the app has one); (2) signing in works; (3) one real write succeeds: create a note, reload, it is still there, delete it; (4) the feature you shipped does what the PR says; (5) the console and Network panel show no new errors or failed requests. If a step fails, roll back first and debug second.

## Why it works

A green pipeline proves the build and tests passed in CI, not that production is set up correctly. Environment variables, migrations, rewrites, and third-party keys only exist in production. A smoke check is a short, fixed list that touches each of those layers once (shallow but broad), so a broken deploy is caught by you in minutes instead of by users.

## Verify it

Keep the list in the repo (for example `docs/smoke-check.md`) and paste the results into the PR or release note. Compare what is deployed with what was merged: the commit label or changed screen should match `git log --oneline -1 origin/main`. Run the list after every deploy, including rollbacks.

cards.front: A users table has UNIQUE (email) and deletes accounts by setting deleted_at. Someone who deleted their account signs up again with the same email and gets 'Email already taken'. What should the schema use instead?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Replace the plain constraint with a partial unique index that covers only live rows: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_active ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;`, then drop the old UNIQUE constraint (in PostgreSQL, `ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT` with the name `\d users` lists, usually `users_email_key`). Two active accounts still cannot share an email, but any number of soft-deleted rows can keep theirs. PostgreSQL 17 and SQLite both support partial indexes.

## Why it works

A UNIQUE constraint compares every row, and a soft-deleted row is still a row, so it holds on to the email forever. A partial index includes only rows matching its WHERE clause, so uniqueness is enforced among `deleted_at IS NULL` rows only. This is one of soft delete's hidden costs: every rule and every query must now say which rows count as live.

## Verify it

In sqlite3, create the table with the partial index, insert ana@x.com, set its deleted_at, and insert ana@x.com again: it succeeds. A third, live ana@x.com fails with "UNIQUE constraint failed: users.email". Also check that the signup code's "email exists?" lookup adds `AND deleted_at IS NULL`, or it will still say taken.

cards.front: A free-text tasks.status column now holds 'done', 'Done', 'DONE ' and 'completed', and the Done filter misses most of them. How do you stop new variants when the existing rows are already messy?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Clean first, then constrain, in one migration: `UPDATE tasks SET status = 'done' WHERE lower(trim(status)) IN ('done', 'completed');` then, in PostgreSQL, `ALTER TABLE tasks ADD CONSTRAINT tasks_status_valid CHECK (status IN ('open', 'done'));`. From then on the database rejects any other spelling, whichever code writes it.

## Why it works

In PostgreSQL, adding a CHECK to an existing table scans the current rows and fails if any row breaks it, which is why the cleanup comes first. API validation covered only one code path; imports, scripts and old app versions wrote the variants. A CHECK list makes the allowed values part of the schema. If the list changes often or needs labels, use a `task_statuses` table and a foreign key instead.

## Verify it

Before the migration, run `SELECT status, count(*) FROM tasks GROUP BY status;` and confirm only 'open' and 'done' remain. Afterwards, in a test database, run `UPDATE tasks SET status = 'Done' WHERE id = 1;` and expect a check-constraint error. SQLite has no ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT, so there the CHECK must be declared in CREATE TABLE (rebuild the table).

cards.front: An orders table keeps its line items in a JSON column like [{"sku":"A1","qty":2}]. Finance wants units sold per SKU last month, and a bug saved a qty of -3 unnoticed. What schema would serve this better?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Move line items into a child table: `order_items (order_id REFERENCES orders (id), sku, qty integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0), unit_price_cents ...)` with an index on `order_id`. The report becomes a plain `GROUP BY sku` over order_items joined to orders, and a negative qty is rejected on insert. Keep JSON for data you always read and write whole and never filter or constrain, such as a raw webhook payload.

## Why it works

Inside one JSON value an item cannot have a foreign key, and giving each item a type, NOT NULL or CHECK rule takes awkward JSON expressions instead of plain column definitions, so bad items get in silently, and every report must first expand the array into rows (PostgreSQL has `jsonb_array_elements` for that). Rows in a child table are what SQL is built to filter, join, sum, index and constrain.

## Verify it

Rehearse the backfill in a test database. In SQLite, `json_each(orders.items)` expands each array into rows you can INSERT into order_items; the -3 item makes that INSERT fail on the CHECK, so fix or exclude it first. Compare `SELECT sku, sum(qty) FROM order_items GROUP BY sku` with the JSON totals before dropping the old column.

cards.front: tasks.project_id was created as a plain integer with no foreign key. A PostgreSQL migration adding REFERENCES projects (id) now fails, because some tasks point at projects that were deleted. What do you do?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Find the orphans, decide what they mean, then add the constraint. `SELECT t.id, t.project_id FROM tasks t LEFT JOIN projects p ON p.id = t.project_id WHERE p.id IS NULL AND t.project_id IS NOT NULL;` lists them. Delete them, move them to an "Unsorted" project, or set project_id to NULL if the column allows it. Then run `ALTER TABLE tasks ADD CONSTRAINT tasks_project_fk FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES projects (id);` and index project_id.

## Why it works

Adding a foreign key makes PostgreSQL scan the existing rows and fail if any row has no matching parent, so the data must be valid first. The orphans exist because nothing ever checked the link, so deleting a project left its tasks behind. Once the constraint exists, the database blocks new orphans. On a big table, `NOT VALID` plus a later `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` defers the scan, but the orphans still have to be fixed.

## Verify it

Run the LEFT JOIN query and expect zero rows before the migration. Afterwards, in a test database, insert a task with project_id 999999 and try deleting a project that still has tasks; both should fail with a foreign-key violation.

cards.front: A tasks table stores due dates as text like '3/14/2026'. Sorting by due_at puts '10/1/2026' before '3/14/2026', and a 'due this week' filter returns the wrong rows. What should the column be?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

A real date type: `due_on date` in PostgreSQL, or `timestamptz` if the time of day matters. Add the new column, fill it by converting the old text with a format pattern (PostgreSQL: `to_date(due_at, 'MM/DD/YYYY')`), confirm every old value got a date, then move the code over. In SQLite, which has no date type, store ISO 8601 text such as '2026-03-14', which sorts correctly as text.

## Why it works

Text compares character by character, so the '1' of '10/1' sorts before the '3' of '3/14', and range filters compare strings, not days. A date column orders and compares by the calendar, only holds real dates, and supports date arithmetic. ISO 8601 text orders correctly because the largest unit comes first and every part has a fixed width.

## Verify it

In sqlite3, `SELECT d FROM t ORDER BY d` over '3/14/2026' and '10/1/2026' returns '10/1/2026' first; the same dates written '2026-03-14' and '2026-10-01' come back in calendar order. After the PostgreSQL backfill, `SELECT count(*) FROM tasks WHERE due_at IS NOT NULL AND due_on IS NULL` should return 0.

cards.front: A dev setup script inserts the roles 'admin' and 'member'. A teammate ran `npm run seed` twice, and the role dropdown now lists every role twice. How should the seed and the roles table change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Make the table reject duplicates and the seed skip existing rows. Delete the duplicates, add `UNIQUE (name)` to roles, and write the seed as `INSERT INTO roles (name) VALUES ('admin'), ('member') ON CONFLICT (name) DO NOTHING;`. Running it once or ten times now leaves the same two rows. The statement works in PostgreSQL and in SQLite 3.24 or later.

## Why it works

A seed loads the reference data the app needs to work, and it is re-run on new laptops, CI databases and after resets, so it must be idempotent: the same result however often it runs. A plain INSERT adds rows every time. Keep fake demo users and sample notes in a separate dev-only script; a production seed holds only real reference data such as roles and statuses.

## Verify it

Run the seed twice against a fresh database, then `SELECT name, count(*) FROM roles GROUP BY name` should show each role with a count of 1. A CI step that seeds twice in a row catches a non-idempotent seed before a teammate does.

cards.front: A task list renders 50 `<TaskRow>`s, and each row's `useEffect` fetches `/api/users/${task.ownerId}` to show the owner's name. The Network panel shows 50 user requests, many for the same user. What should change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Stop fetching per row. Have the list endpoint return what the rows display, for example join users in the tasks query and include `ownerName`, or fetch the owners once in the parent (`GET /api/users?ids=3,8,12`) and pass each row its owner. The page then makes one or two requests instead of 51, and `TaskRow` just renders props.

## Why it works

This is the N+1 problem moved into the browser: one request for the list, then one per row, each with its own HTTP overhead and each starting only when its component mounts. With 20 distinct owners among 50 tasks, a React 19 test counted 50 requests for 20 distinct URLs, so 30 fetched someone already fetched. In development, StrictMode runs each effect twice, doubling the count again.

## Verify it

Reload with the Network panel filtered to `/api/users`: before the fix there is one request per row, after it none or one. A `Server-Timing` query count on `GET /api/tasks` should stay the same when the page size grows from 20 to 50.

cards.front: A newest-first feed appends each "Load more" page with `setTasks(prev => [...prev, ...page])`. After someone adds a task, the next page repeats a task already shown, and React warns about duplicate keys. Why?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The new task pushed every row down one place, so the next page, fetched by position (such as OFFSET 20), starts with the row that ended the previous page. Merge by id when appending: skip items whose id is already in the list. Also disable "Load more" while a page is loading, so a double tap can't append the same page twice.

## Why it works

The server decides page boundaries when each request runs, not when the first page was shown, and blind appending assumes nothing changed in between. In a test with pages of 3, adding task 11 after page one gave `10 9 8 8 7 6`; merging by id gave `10 9 8 7 6`, and React logged "Encountered two children with the same key" for the first list. Merging removes repeats; asking for rows after the last id shown also stops rows being skipped after deletes.

## Verify it

In a test, load page one, insert a task, load the next page, and assert the ids are unique: `new Set(ids).size === ids.length`. In the browser, the duplicate-key warning should be gone from the Console, and double-tapping "Load more" should send a single request in the Network panel.

cards.front: An orders list shows "Page 1 of 4,210". `Server-Timing` on `GET /api/orders` reports `count;dur=1150` next to `rows;dur=4`, and users only ever click Next. What should the endpoint do instead?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Drop the exact total from the list request. Fetch `LIMIT 21` for a page of 20 and return `hasMore`, and show Next or "Load more" instead of "Page 1 of 4,210". If the UI really needs a size, show an approximate figure (for a whole table, PostgreSQL's estimate in `pg_class.reltuples`) or load the exact count in a separate, cached request that doesn't hold up the page.

## Why it works

An exact `COUNT(*)` has to visit every matching row. The PostgreSQL wiki explains that under MVCC it must check each row's visibility, so the cost grows with the table, while fetching 21 rows stops early. In SQLite, on 2 million orders with an index on `(status, id)`, counting the 1,333,333 paid orders took over half a second in two separate runs, while the 21-row page took under 2 ms.
