## Verify it

Compare `Server-Timing` before and after: the count entry is gone, and the handler's time should stay flat as orders are added. Test the edge case: with exactly 40 matching orders, page 2 returns 20 rows and `hasMore: false`.

cards.front: `tasks` has an index on `(owner_id, due_date)`. A new admin page lists all overdue tasks with `WHERE due_date < ? ORDER BY due_date LIMIT 50` and is slow. Why doesn't the index help, and what do you add?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

The index is sorted by `owner_id` first and by `due_date` only within each owner, so a query with no `owner_id` condition can't jump to "due before X": those dates are scattered through the whole index. Add an index that leads with the filtered column: `CREATE INDEX tasks_due ON tasks (due_date)`. Keep the old one, because owner-scoped queries still use it.

## Why it works

A multicolumn B-tree narrows its search with equality on the leading columns plus a range on the next one. The PostgreSQL 17 docs say that without a condition on the first column the entire index would have to be scanned, so the planner usually reads the table instead. PostgreSQL 18 added B-tree skip scan, which helps in some such cases. SQLite can skip-scan after `ANALYZE` when `owner_id` has few distinct values, but it still sorts afterwards; an index led by `due_date` avoids both.

## Verify it

In SQLite (before any `ANALYZE`), `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for the query showed `SCAN tasks` and `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`; after adding `tasks_due` it showed `SEARCH tasks USING INDEX tasks_due (due_date<?)` with no temp sort. In PostgreSQL, run `EXPLAIN` and look for an index scan on `tasks_due` instead of a Seq Scan followed by a Sort.

cards.front: A product page's hero is a 4000×3000 JPEG of 3.1 MB, shown 400 CSS pixels wide on phones. On mobile data it appears last, and the text below jumps down when it loads. What do you change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Serve sizes that match the display: export a few widths (say 480, 800 and 1600 px) and list them in `srcset` with `w` descriptors plus a `sizes` attribute, so a phone downloads a small file. Use a modern format such as WebP or AVIF where you can. Add `width="1600" height="1200"` (the image's ratio) or CSS `aspect-ratio` so the browser reserves the space before the image arrives.

## Why it works

With `srcset` and `sizes`, the browser works out how wide the slot is and loads the listed file that fits it, taking screen density into account (MDN, Responsive images), so a 400-px slot doesn't pull a 4000-px file. Modern browsers derive an image's aspect ratio from its `width` and `height` attributes before it loads (web.dev, Optimize CLS), so the text keeps its place.

## Verify it

In DevTools device mode with a phone size, filter the Network panel to Img: the hero request should be one of the smaller files, far below 3.1 MB. Record in the Performance panel while loading and check that no layout shift is reported when the image appears.

cards.front: `vite build` shows the main chunk grew by about 70 kB after a teammate added `import _ from 'lodash'` just to call `_.debounce`. How do you get the helper without the whole library?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer

Import only the function: `import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'` (a one-function file), or switch to `lodash-es` and write `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'`, which the bundler can tree-shake. For one small helper, writing your own 8-line debounce is also fine. Rebuild and compare the chunk size.

## Why it works

The `lodash` entry point is one big CommonJS file, so the bundler can't drop the parts you don't use; even `import { debounce } from 'lodash'` pulled in the whole library. In one test build with Rolldown 1.1 (the bundler inside Vite 8) and lodash 4, minified, the default and named imports both came to about 70 kB (25 kB gzipped), `lodash/debounce` to 3.2 kB and `lodash-es` to 2.2 kB. Exact sizes vary by version and bundler.

## Verify it

Run `vite build` before and after the change and compare the size and gzip size printed for the main `index-<hash>.js` chunk. Then check that search still waits for the user to stop typing, so the smaller import behaves the same.
